(CNN) -- The September issue of Essence magazine features an interview with Sen. Barack Obama and his family inside their Chicago home. Angela Burt-Murray is editor-in-chief of Essence magazine. Essence editor-in-chief Angela Burt-Murray said it took a year for the magazine to gain access to the Obama's Illinois home for an intimate interview with the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee, his wife, Michelle, and their daughters, Sasha and Malia. Burt-Murray talked Thursday with CNN "American Morning" anchor Kiran Chetry about the interview and the Obama family. Chetry: You are the first African-American media outlet to get this inside look. Did your team get a chance to see the real Obamas? Burt-Murray: I think we did. We went to their home on the South Side of Chicago and it was wonderful to see them as a family interacting with each other, and see the girls skipping around the house, just acting like it's a normal, everyday occurrence to have a camera crew in their home and Secret Service at different points throughout the house and around the yard. But it didn't really seem to impact the girls in any way.  Watch what Essence found inside the Obamas' home » . Chetry: Much was made of an earlier televised interview they with their daughters and they said, looking back, they probably shouldn't have done that. There is so much interest about their family, and yet they want to protect their girls. How do they balance that? Burt-Murray: They try to take a look at who is around the family and make sure they try to keep things as structured as possible. But also, you have instances where magazines like Essence show up to take photographs, but the girls are very relaxed because they're in their home environment. And I think that's the difference between our photo shoot and what you saw on television. Taking the girls outside of their home and putting them in the spotlight is probably a bit more challenging for them as parents. Chetry: They have to deal with completing stereotypes, if you will: They were parodied as these angry black radicals and as these Ivy League elitists. In the magazine, Gwen Ifill wrote, "The Obamas pride themselves on creating a family picture that is authentically black with shades of Norman Rockwell." Explain that. How are they getting that image out. Burt-Murray: I think it's the idea that they're just an average American family. They have strong family values, they're deeply rooted in their community and they want to show their girls a great example of achievement. But they also want to be a model for the rest of their community. The Obamas talk about in our story how important it is for them to continue to live in their South Side Chicago neighborhood because it's a neighborhood in transition. So you have children who have the opportunity to see an African-American man run for the highest office in the nation right in their neighborhood. So they're modeling not only for their children but also for the larger community. Chetry: They do live in a gated community, a $1.6 million home, so it's out of reach for a lot of people. Burt-Murray: But it's so accessible. While we were there photographing them for Essence, you could see the cars going by and stopping and people getting out to take photographs. The girls were on the porch and people could see them. There is some normalcy there, but it's also obviously something very special and different. Chetry: They said race had been prominent on the campaign trail. Barack Obama told Gwen Ifill that he thinks race is a national obsession. He thinks the racial divide is not as big an issue in this country as it's made out to be. Burt-Murray: As evidenced by the success that he's had with his campaign, you can certainly see that attitudes are shifting. But there are still challenges, obviously, that need to be addressed. And it keeps coming up throughout the campaign. So it will be interesting to see what happens when the country goes to the polls in November.

**Burt-Murray:** I believe we did. **Chetry:** A great deal was made of an earlier televised interview involving their daughters, and they later reflected that, in hindsight, they probably shouldn't have done it. There is tremendous interest in their family, and yet they wish to protect their girls. How do they strike that balance?

**Chetry:** They must contend with competing stereotypes, if you will: they have been caricatured as angry black radicals on one hand and as Ivy League elitists on the other. **Burt-Murray:** I think it stems from the notion that they are simply an average American family. They hold strong family values, they are deeply rooted in their community, and they want to set a great example of achievement for their girls. counterfactuals.output:
# One-on-One: Essence Editor on Obama Family Cover Story

*The following is an edited transcript from CNN's "American Morning."*

---

**ANCHOR:** Welcome back to "American Morning." This September, Essence magazine is giving readers an intimate look at Senator Barack Obama and his family at their Chicago home. Joining us now is the editor-in-chief of Essence magazine. Thanks so much for being here.

**EDITOR-IN-CHIEF:** Thank you for having me. It's a pleasure.

**ANCHOR:** So let's start with the big question—how did this cover story come together? What made you decide to feature the Obamas this month?

**EDITOR-IN-CHIEF:** Well, our readers have been telling us for months how invested they are in this election, and in Senator Obama's candidacy specifically. We wanted to go beyond the stump speeches and the policy debates and really introduce our audience to the Obamas as a family. We sat down with them in their home in Chicago, and what emerged was a really warm, revealing portrait.

**ANCHOR:** And you spoke with both the senator and Michelle Obama?

**EDITOR-IN-CHIEF:** We did. And I have to say, one of the most striking things was seeing them together as partners. Michelle is remarkably candid, and she talks about the challenges of balancing family life with the demands of a national campaign. Their daughters came up quite a bit—how they're trying to keep things normal for the girls.

**ANCHOR:** That's something a lot of families can relate to, that work-life balance. Did the conversation stay personal, or did you get into some of the political issues as well?

**EDITOR-IN-CHIEF:** It was a real mix. Naturally, we talked about the issues that matter most to our readership—education, the economy, health care, the state of the African-American community. But what makes this piece different is the personal texture. You get a sense of who they are when the cameras are off. There's a photo spread that captures them at home, relaxed, and I think readers will feel like they're getting to know a real family.

**ANCHOR:** Let me ask you about the significance here. Essence has a predominantly African-American readership. What does it mean to feature a candidate who could become the first black president?

**EDITOR-IN-CHIEF:** It's historic, and we don't take that lightly. For our readers, this moment carries enormous weight. But I want to be clear—we approached this as a journalistic endeavor, not an endorsement. Our job is to inform our audience and let them make their own decisions. That said, there's no denying the emotional resonance this candidacy has for the community we serve.

**ANCHOR:** Some critics might say a glowing family profile amounts to favorable coverage. How do you respond to that?

**EDITOR-IN-CHIEF:** It's a fair question, and I'd say this: a profile is not an endorsement. We ask tough questions, and we hold public figures accountable regardless of who they are. Our readers are sophisticated. They can appreciate a personal story while still scrutinizing a candidate's positions. We'd extend the same opportunity to any candidate who wanted to speak directly to our audience.

**ANCHOR:** Before we let you go—what's the one thing you hope readers take away from this cover story?

**EDITOR-IN-CHIEF:** I hope they come away feeling like they understand the Obamas a little better, not just as political figures, but as people. Whatever your politics, there's value in seeing the human side of the people who want to lead this country. That's what we set out to capture.

**ANCHOR:** The September issue of Essence magazine, on newsstands now. Thank you so much for joining us this morning.

**EDITOR-IN-CHIEF:** Thank you. It was a pleasure.

**ANCHOR:** We'll be right back after this break.

---

*© Cable News Network. This transcript has been edited for clarity.*

counterfactuals.output:
# Behind the Headlines: Protecting the First Family's Youngest Members

*An interview with Diane Whitmore, Managing Editor of American Family Magazine, conducted during the 2008 presidential campaign*

---

**Q: You've covered political families for over two decades. How does the Obama campaign's approach to their daughters compare to what you've seen before?**

**Whitmore:** What strikes me most is the deliberateness of it. Barack and Michelle have drawn very clear lines. Malia and Sasha are ten and seven right now, and the campaign has essentially declared them off-limits for the kind of coverage that would exploit their childhood. That's not entirely new—most candidates want to shield their kids—but the Obamas have been unusually explicit about it.

**Q: Can you give an example of where those lines have been tested?**

**Whitmore:** The most talked-about moment was the family's interview with *Access Hollywood* back in July. The girls participated, they were charming and candid, and audiences loved it. But afterward, Barack himself expressed regret about it. He said something to the effect that he and Michelle didn't want to make a habit of it—that it was a mistake to put the children in that spotlight. That's remarkable, actually. A candidate publicly second-guessing a piece of favorable coverage because it involved his daughters.

**Q: Why do you think they reversed course so publicly?**

**Whitmore:** I think they recognized the trap. Positive coverage is still coverage, and every appearance normalizes the idea that these children are public figures. Once you invite cameras into your kids' lives voluntarily, it becomes much harder to object when the press wants access later. They were setting a precedent—and they realized it was the wrong one.

**Q: There's an obvious tension here. Voters want to know who these candidates are as people, and family is central to that. How do you reconcile the public's legitimate interest with a child's right to privacy?**

**Whitmore:** That's the essential question, and I don't think there's a clean answer. The public interest in a candidate's *character* is real. How someone parents, how they talk about their family, the values they model—that's genuinely relevant to understanding the person who might hold the office. But there's a difference between the parents *telling* us about their family and turning the children themselves into props or performers. Michelle draws that distinction well. She'll talk about her daughters, about the challenges of raising them while campaigning, but she's guarding the actual children.

**Q: Michelle Obama has spoken about wanting to keep their lives normal. Is that even possible on a national campaign?**

**Whitmore:** Realistically? Only partially. But she's fighting hard for it. From what we understand, the girls keep their routines—school, activities, bedtimes. Michelle has scaled back her own schedule to be home. She's talked about being "mom-in-chief" first. There's a real effort to make sure the campaign happens around the children's lives, not the other way around. Whether that survives an actual presidency is another matter entirely.

**Q: If they win, the scrutiny only intensifies. Do you think this protective posture is sustainable in the White House?**

**Whitmore:** It gets much harder. The White House press corps is relentless, and a First Family's children become objects of enormous curiosity. But there's actually a long tradition of the press extending some courtesy to presidential children—it goes back through the Clinton and Carter years. When Chelsea Clinton was young, there was a broad understanding that she'd be left alone. I'd expect the Obamas to lean on that tradition and enforce it firmly. Michelle strikes me as someone who will not budge on this.

**Q: As a journalist yourself, where do you personally land on this? Isn't the press entitled to cover a public family?**

**Whitmore:** I land on the side of the children, frankly. The candidates chose this life; their kids didn't. My view is that we cover the parents fully—their record, their judgment, their character—and we leave the children their childhood. When a candidate voluntarily features their kids, we can report on it. But we shouldn't manufacture demand for access to seven-year-olds. That's not journalism serving the public; that's journalism serving curiosity, and those aren't the same thing.

**Q: Any final thoughts on what this tells us about the Obamas?**

**Whitmore:** I think how a family handles this pressure is revealing in itself. The willingness to forgo favorable coverage to protect your kids—that tells you something about priorities. Whatever voters ultimately decide about the politics, the instinct to shield those two girls is one of the more human threads running through this whole campaign.

---

*This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.*

*A new profile explores the family's roots, values, and connection to Chicago's South Side*

In a deeply personal profile, Essence magazine has pulled back the curtain on Barack and Michelle Obama, offering readers a glimpse into the couple's family life, their reflections on race in America, and their enduring ties to Chicago's South Side.

The feature, which combines candid conversation with reflective commentary, presents the Obamas not just as public figures but as partners navigating parenthood, career, and their place in a rapidly changing national conversation about identity.

## Roots in the South Side

Central to the profile is the couple's relationship to Chicago's South Side, the historically Black neighborhood that shaped Michelle Obama's upbringing and became a foundation for the family's identity.

The area, long known for its rich cultural legacy alongside its economic challenges, is described in the piece as more than a backdrop. For the Obamas, it represents community, resilience, and the working-class values that both credit with grounding them.

Michelle Obama, who grew up in the neighborhood, speaks about the tight-knit community that raised her and the lessons in perseverance that came from watching her parents work to provide opportunities for their children.

## Reflections on Race

The profile does not shy away from discussions of race, a subject the Obamas have approached throughout their public lives with a mix of candor and caution.

The couple reflects on what it means to represent a barrier-breaking moment in American history while also acknowledging the complexities and expectations that accompany such visibility. They discuss the importance of speaking honestly about race while working to build bridges across communities.

Essence, which has long served as a leading voice for Black women in America, provides a fitting platform for these conversations, allowing the Obamas to speak directly to a readership that has followed their journey closely.

## Family First

Throughout the profile, family values emerge as a recurring theme. The Obamas emphasize the priority they place on raising their daughters with a strong sense of self and an appreciation for hard work.

The couple describes efforts to maintain a sense of normalcy amid the pressures of public life—shared meals, established routines, and honest conversations about the world their children are inheriting.

Their partnership, both personal and professional, is portrayed as a source of strength, with each crediting the other for support through demanding chapters of their lives.

## A Personal Portrait

What distinguishes the Essence profile is its intimacy. Rather than focusing solely on policy or politics, the piece invites readers into the more human dimensions of the Obamas' story—their humor, their occasional disagreements, and the values that anchor them.

For a family that has often lived under intense scrutiny, the profile represents an opportunity to speak in their own words, on their own terms, to a magazine and a community that has embraced their story.

The feature is available in the latest issue of Essence magazine.

# Race, Identity, and Image: A Newsroom Conversation

*The following is a framed editorial interview exploring media coverage themes during a historic campaign. The participants are fictional composites representing common newsroom perspectives of the era.*

---

**EDITOR:** Thanks for sitting down with me. When we look back at how the coverage unfolded, one thing stands out—the constant negotiation over how to talk about race. From your anchor chair, how did you approach that?

**ANCHOR:** Carefully, and never perfectly. The challenge was that race was simultaneously everywhere and nowhere in this campaign. Everyone could see the historic dimension—the possibility of the first Black president—but the campaign itself often tried to keep race at arm's length. So we were narrating something the candidate wasn't necessarily centering.

**EDITOR:** Let's talk about that phrase—"the first Black president." Did you ever feel that framing flattened the story?

**ANCHOR:** All the time. There's a shorthand danger in media. We reach for the milestone because it's clear, it's dramatic, it fits a headline. But "first Black president" can reduce a complicated person to a category. Here was a candidate with a Kenyan father and a white mother from Kansas, raised partly in Indonesia and Hawaii. His biography didn't fit the traditional narrative of Black America shaped by slavery and the civil rights movement.

**EDITOR:** Which raised the "is he Black enough?" question that got a lot of airtime.

**ANCHOR:** And I have mixed feelings about how we handled it. On one hand, it was a genuine conversation happening in Black communities—about authenticity, about shared historical experience, about whether someone had to descend from enslaved Americans to represent that legacy. That's a legitimate discussion. On the other hand, cable news sometimes weaponized it, turning a nuanced identity question into a cynical horse-race angle: "Will Black voters trust him?"

**EDITOR:** How do you cover an authentic community debate without exploiting it?

**ANCHOR:** You bring in voices from inside the community rather than talking about them from the anchor desk. You resist the urge to declare a verdict at the end of the segment. Identity isn't a poll number. The mistake we made repeatedly was treating "Black identity" as monolithic—as if there were one Black opinion to be won or lost.

---

**EDITOR:** Stereotypes became a real minefield. There was the "angry Black man" trope lurking behind coverage of his tone, and later the caricatures aimed at his wife.

**ANCHOR:** This is where I think media self-awareness mattered most. The candidate had to perform a very specific kind of restraint. He couldn't show anger—not about race, not about attacks—because the stereotype of the threatening Black man was always waiting to be triggered. Commentators praised him as "cool" and "professorial," and those words were coded. The subtext was: *he's not scary.* We rarely interrogated our own praise.

**EDITOR:** Say more about that.

**ANCHOR:** When we complimented his calm, we were often revealing the assumption underneath—that calmness was noteworthy, even surprising, in a Black man seeking power. The stereotype shaped the compliment as much as the criticism. A white candidate showing passion is "fired up." A Black candidate showing the same might be "aggressive." We should have named that dynamic on air more often instead of participating in it.

**EDITOR:** And his wife faced a sharper version of this.

**ANCHOR:** Much sharper. She was a Princeton and Harvard Law graduate, an accomplished professional—and yet she got caricatured as angry, unpatriotic, militant. A single comment about being proud of her country got looped endlessly. There's a long, ugly history in this country of casting Black women as angry or emasculating, and some of the coverage tapped straight into that vein, sometimes without the people producing it even realizing it.

**EDITOR:** Did the campaign respond by reshaping her image?

**ANCHOR:** Deliberately. You saw a pivot toward softer, family-centered imagery—the mom-in-chief framing, appearances on daytime television, emphasis on their daughters. It was a strategic reassurance campaign. And here's the tension I always felt: was that a dignified reclaiming of their own story, or was it a capitulation to stereotypes that demanded a Black family prove its wholesomeness in ways white families never had to?

---

**EDITOR:** That family image became almost a counter-narrative in itself.

**ANCHOR:** It did, and it was powerful. Two parents, two kids, visible affection, an intact and aspirational household. For many Black viewers, especially, seeing that family on the national stage was profoundly moving—a rebuttal to decades of media that overwhelmingly showed Black families as broken or in crisis.

**EDITOR:** But you're uneasy about it.

**ANCHOR:** I'm uneasy about *why* it had to work so hard. The wholesome family functioned partly as armor against suspicion—against the whisper campaigns, the false rumors about his faith, his birthplace, his patriotism. The image had to constantly say, *we are safe, we are American, we belong.* No candidate should have to spend that much energy proving their belonging. That burden was racialized.

**EDITOR:** Those rumors you mention—the false claims about religion and birthplace. How should newsrooms have handled them?

**ANCHOR:** That's one of our clearest failures and lessons. Early on, too many outlets covered the rumors as controversy—"some people are saying"—which amplified lies under the cover of reporting the debate. Repeating a falsehood to debunk it can still cement it in people's minds. We learned, slowly, that the responsible move was to state the fact plainly and not give equal time to bad-faith fabrication. But the damage of that "just asking questions" framing lingered for years.

---

**EDITOR:** Let's talk about the speech on race—the one prompted by the controversy over his former pastor. That was a moment the media couldn't sidestep race.

**ANCHOR:** No, and it forced a reckoning. Suddenly the candidate who had run a campaign that transcended race had to address it head-on, because incendiary sermon clips demanded a response. What struck me was that he refused the easy path. He didn't simply denounce and move on. He tried to explain the anger in those pews as rooted in real historical grievance, while also naming resentments among white working-class Americans. He treated the audience as adults.

**EDITOR:** Did the media treat the audience as adults?

**ANCHOR:** Unevenly. Some of us ran the full speech and let it breathe. Others chopped it into the most inflammatory soundbites. That split tells you everything about the two modes of coverage available to us—one that trusts complexity, one that feeds conflict. Ratings often rewarded the second mode. That's an uncomfortable admission.

---

**EDITOR:** Looking back, what's the lesson for how we cover race and identity in politics going forward?

**ANCHOR:** A few things. First, stop treating any racial group as a single voting bloc with a single opinion. Second, interrogate our own language—the coded compliments, the surprised tone, the words we reserve for candidates of color. Third, be honest that "objectivity" can hide our assumptions rather than remove them. And finally, resist the milestone trap. The historic "first" is real and worth honoring, but a person is not a symbol. When we reduce someone to what they represent, we stop covering who they actually are and what they'd actually do.

**EDITOR:** Any regret that stays with you?

**ANCHOR:** That we spent so much time asking whether America was ready for a Black president, and comparatively little asking why that was the question we felt entitled to ask. The framing itself carried a bias—it centered the comfort of some voters over the qualifications of the candidate. If I could redo my segments, I'd turn that question around more often. Not "is the country ready?" but "what does our anxiety about readiness reveal about us?"

**EDITOR:** That feels like a good place to end.

**ANCHOR:** It's a good place to keep starting, actually. These questions didn't get resolved. They just moved to the next campaign.

---

*This dialogue is a fictional editorial exercise designed to surface media-criticism themes—identity, stereotype, and representation—rather than a transcript of any real interview.*
